author: Keystone Today
title: Philadelphia restaurateur indicted for employment tax fraud in federal case
text:
← Back to the wire
Philadelphia restaurateur indicted for employment tax fraud in federal case
Charles Weiner has been indicted on multiple federal charges related to employment tax fraud involving his Philadelphia restaurants. The case is part of a broader Department of Justice enforcement effort targeting alleged large-scale tax crimes nationwide.
Charles Weiner, 79, of Penn Valley, Pennsylvania, was charged by indictment with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States, 22 counts of willful failure to withhold and pay over employment taxes, and six counts of aiding and assisting the filing of false tax returns, according to an Oct. 15 announcement from U.S. Attorney David Metcalf.
The indictment is part of the Department of Justice’s first-ever National Tax Enforcement Surge, a month-long initiative involving the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices across the country. The surge resulted in prosecutorial actions against 76 defendants whose alleged and proven crimes intended an estimated loss of revenue to the federal government exceeding $490 million.
According to details provided in the indictment, Weiner owned two restaurants on Germantown Avenue in Philadelphia: Max’s Steaks & Eagle Bar and Clock Bar. He managed all financial matters related to these businesses and was responsible for withholding Social Security, Medicare, and income taxes from employees’ wages as well as filing quarterly employment tax returns with the Internal Revenue Service.
The indictment alleges that between early 2019 through early 2023, Weiner and two others working at his direction paid restaurant employees all or partly in cash while providing only partial wage information to their accountant. As a result, false quarterly tax returns were filed with the IRS during this period. The indictment further alleges that Weiner supplied false information regarding food and drink supply purchases for his restaurants so that annual corporate tax returns would also be inaccurate.
If convicted on all charges, Weiner faces up to five years in prison for conspiracy; five years per count for willful failure to withhold and pay over employment taxes; and three years per count for aiding or assisting in filing false tax returns.
The Department of Justice created its National Fraud Enforcement Division on April 7, 2026. Its mission is "to zealously investigate and prosecute those who steal or fraudulently misuse taxpayer dollars." Efforts by this division support President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud—a whole-of-government initiative chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance aimed at eliminating fraud within federal benefit programs.
This case was investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation agents. It is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Eric D. Gill, along with Trial Attorney Michael C. Vasiliadis from the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Tax Section.
Authorities emphasized that charges contained in indictments are accusations only; every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
